pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 12–13 years

- **Topic:** Efficiency, Sankey diagrams, and work done

- **Standards — UK (DfE National Curriculum, England):** this is KS4 (GCSE) content (late-KS3 lead-in). KS4 Physics 'Energy' (statutory, verified): 'calculating energy efficiency for any energy transfers' and 'conservation of energy in a closed system, dissipation'; KS4 Forces (statutory): 'calculating work done as force x distance'. KS3 carries only the qualitative precursors ('total energy has the same value before and after a change'; 'simple machines… product of force and displacement unchanged'). Sankey diagrams are the standard GCSE representation though not named in statute.

- **Standards — US NATIONAL (NGSS):** efficiency/quantitative energy modelling is HS, not MS — HS-PS3-1 (computational model of energy in a system) and HS-PS3-3 (design a device that works within constraints, accounting for efficiency); MS has no efficiency PE. Builds on 'Energy can't be created or destroyed'; needs percentage skills.

- **Operational details:** A PROCEDURAL topic spanning three linked calculations/representations: efficiency = useful output energy ÷ total input energy (as a ratio/percentage), constructing and interpreting Sankey diagrams (arrow WIDTH proportional to energy, total in = total out), and work done = force × distance (joules). This is genuinely quantitative — percentages, proportional drawing, and a formula — and rests on conservation/dissipation (no real device is 100% efficient; the 'wasted' energy is dissipated, usually to the thermal store of the surroundings, NOT destroyed).

- **Checkpoint:** Tier C (formal/quantitative, age 12-13).
bestPractices: Anchor efficiency in conservation FIRST: total input = useful output + wasted (dissipated) energy, so efficiency is the fraction that ends up useful; this makes >100% impossible and explains why the 'wasted' arrow must exist.

Build Sankey diagrams from the conservation constraint: the input arrow's width must equal the sum of the output arrows' widths — draw to scale (e.g. 1 cm = 10 J) so the proportionality is real, not decorative, and the widths visibly balance.

Teach 'useful vs wasted' as CONTEXT-dependent, not intrinsic: a lamp's thermal output is wasted, a heater's thermal output is useful — the same transfer is useful or wasted depending on the device's purpose.

Define work done operationally and confront the everyday meaning: W = Fd is energy transferred when a force moves through a distance IN ITS DIRECTION; holding a heavy bag still (no movement) does NO work in physics, even though it feels effortful.
Separate the trio of confusable quantities — work/energy (J), force (N), and (next topic) power (W) — with units and worked examples, since students blur them.
keyRepresentations: A to-scale Sankey diagram (input arrow splitting into a useful branch and a wasted/dissipated branch; widths summing to the input).
The efficiency bar/ratio: useful output as a fraction of total input, shown as a percentage.
The conservation ledger: input = useful + wasted, with the wasted share labelled 'dissipated to surroundings (thermal)'.
A work-done diagram: a force arrow moving an object through a distance, W = F × d with units (N × m = J).
commonMisconceptions: 'Wasted energy is lost/destroyed' — it is dissipated (spread out, usually to the thermal store of the surroundings), still conserved; the Sankey's wasted arrow accounts for it.
Drawing Sankey arrows not to scale, or with output widths that don't sum to the input — breaking conservation in the representation.
Believing a device can be >100% efficient, or that a more efficient device 'creates' or 'saves' energy rather than wasting less of it.
Thinking 'useful' vs 'wasted' is a fixed property of an energy type rather than depending on the device's purpose.
Work-done errors: counting work when there is no movement (holding still), using the wrong (perpendicular) distance, or conflating work, force and power.

learn.summary: For ages 12–13 (GCSE lead-in / NGSS HS placement), this procedural topic covers three linked quantitative skills: efficiency = useful output ÷ total input (as a ratio/percentage), constructing and interpreting to-scale Sankey diagrams, and work done = force × distance (joules). All three rest on conservation of energy and dissipation: no real device is 100% efficient, and 'wasted' energy is dissipated (usually to the thermal store of the surroundings), not destroyed. The core activity is a build-and-calculate bench where learners set an input, drag the useful/wasted split, see arrows redraw to scale and an efficiency readout update, plus a work-done tool linking force and distance to W = Fd. Reading-a-Sankey reference, calculation practice, and predict-then-check problems support this.

activities.title: Sankey-and-efficiency bench: build energy transfers to scale
feedback: If a learner tries to exceed 100%: the useful output can never be larger than the total input — the wasted branch can shrink toward zero, but total out cannot exceed total in.
If branch widths don't sum to the input: set a scale (e.g. 1 cm = 10 J), measure each arrow, and check useful + wasted adds back to the input — energy is conserved.
If arrows are drawn the same width for different values (e.g. 60 J and 40 J): the width must be proportional to the energy, so the 60 J arrow should be wider than the 40 J one.
If a learner says wasted energy is lost: ask where the 40 J actually goes — it spreads out to the thermal store of the surroundings and is still accounted for on the diagram.
activities.rationale: Building the Sankey from the conservation constraint, with widths that must sum to the input and an efficiency cap at 100%, confronts the 'wasted = destroyed' and non-proportional-arrow misconceptions directly and makes the quantitative relationships concrete. The live recompute and drag-the-split interactions are optional means of making the proportionality and ceiling tangible.
sourceClaims: Students treat 'wasted' energy as destroyed rather than dissipated, draw non-proportional Sankey arrows that break conservation, and count work done when there is no movement.
learnerActions: Set a device's input energy (e.g. 100 J into a motor).
Drag the split between the useful output branch and the wasted (dissipated) branch; watch the arrow widths redraw to scale in real time.
Read the live efficiency meter showing useful ÷ total as a percentage.
Try to drag the useful arrow wider than the input — notice it cannot exceed the input, and efficiency cannot pass 100%.
Observe the wasted branch labelled 'dissipated to surroundings (thermal)' peeling off rather than vanishing.
Check that the useful and wasted branch widths sum back to the input width every time.
Work predict-then-check problems: predict the efficiency and arrow widths, then set the split and compare.
activities.intendedInsight: Efficiency is the fraction of input energy that ends up useful; input = useful + wasted, so efficiency can never exceed 100% and 'wasted' energy is dissipated, not destroyed. Drawing arrow widths in proportion makes conservation visible rather than decorative.

activities.title: Work done = force × distance: make W = Fd a felt quantity
feedback: If a learner claims work is done while holding something still: no distance moved means W = F × 0 = 0 J of work done on the load; the physics definition requires movement in the force's direction. Your muscles still transfer energy inside your body (it ends up dissipated thermally), which is why holding feels tiring, but that energy is not work done on the load.
If the wrong (perpendicular) distance is used: match the distance to the direction the force acts in.
If units are dropped: force in newtons × distance in metres gives work in joules (N·m = J).
activities.rationale: Defining work operationally and explicitly confronting the everyday meaning ('holding a heavy bag does no work') addresses a documented error of counting work with no movement, and keeps work/energy (J) distinct from force (N).
sourceClaims: Students treat 'wasted' energy as destroyed rather than dissipated, draw non-proportional Sankey arrows that break conservation, and count work done when there is no movement.
learnerActions: Push an object (e.g. a crate) with a force arrow through a distance; watch W = F × d accumulate with units (N × m = J).
Adjust force and distance (e.g. sliders) and observe how W changes.
Compute a worked case: W = 20 N × 2 m = 40 J, stating units.
Test the 'holding still' case: keep the load stationary and see that zero distance gives zero work, even though holding feels effortful.
Check that the distance used is the distance moved in the direction of the force, not a perpendicular distance.
activities.intendedInsight: Work done is energy transferred when a force moves an object through a distance in the force's direction; no movement means no work in physics, which contrasts with the everyday sense of 'effort'.

activities.title: Useful vs wasted depends on the device's purpose
feedback: If a learner treats thermal energy as always wasted: ask what the device is for — a heater's thermal output is exactly its useful job.
If a learner treats 'useful' as intrinsic to the energy type: the classification follows the device's purpose, so compare the lamp and the heater to see the same transfer switch roles.
activities.rationale: Treating useful/wasted as context-dependent addresses the misconception that these labels are intrinsic to an energy type; the lamp-vs-heater contrast is a specific, well-chosen example.
learnerActions: Compare two devices: a lamp (whose thermal output is wasted) and a heater (whose thermal output is useful).
For each, label the same type of transfer as useful or wasted according to what the device is for.
State the device's purpose and then decide which output branch of its Sankey is 'useful'.
activities.intendedInsight: 'Useful' and 'wasted' are not fixed properties of an energy type — the same thermal output can be useful or wasted depending on what the device is meant to do.

activities.title: Read and interpret a given Sankey diagram
feedback: If a learner picks a diagram where outputs don't sum to the input: that breaks conservation — the branches must add back to the input.
If a branch is mislabelled: relate the branch to the device's purpose to decide useful vs wasted.
activities.rationale: Reading practice builds the interpretation evidence (identifying useful/wasted branches, checking balance) and serves as a reference scaffold. On its own, reading a fixed diagram does not give construct-and-calculate practice, so it supplements rather than replaces the building activity.
sourceClaims: Students treat 'wasted' energy as destroyed rather than dissipated, draw non-proportional Sankey arrows that break conservation, and count work done when there is no movement.
learnerActions: Examine a labelled Sankey diagram (e.g. tap branches to reveal energy values and useful/wasted labels).
Identify which branch is the useful output and which is wasted/dissipated.
Explain why the input arrow's width equals the sum of the output arrows' widths.
Spot the error: given several Sankey diagrams, pick the one that conserves energy and say what is wrong with the others (e.g. outputs that don't sum to the input).
activities.intendedInsight: Reading a Sankey means recognising that arrow width represents energy amount, that each branch is useful or wasted, and that total in must equal total out.

activities.title: Consolidate with calculation practice
feedback: If efficiency comes out over 100%: efficiency is useful ÷ total, and since useful output can never exceed total input the result cannot exceed 100% — an over-100% result usually means the ratio has been inverted (total placed on top), so check the values and put useful ÷ total.
If W = Fd is applied with the wrong distance or with no movement: recheck that the distance is moved in the force's direction and is non-zero.
activities.rationale: Mixed calculation and spot-the-error items assess the procedural outcomes efficiently. These recognition/calculation items check fluency but do not by themselves require learners to construct a scaled diagram from scratch.
sourceClaims: KS4 Physics 'Energy' statutory: 'calculating energy efficiency for any energy transfers'; 'conservation of energy in a closed system, dissipation'. KS4 Forces statutory: 'calculating work done as force x distance'. KS3 carries qualitative precursors only.
learnerActions: Calculate efficiency as a percentage from given input and useful output values, placing useful energy over total input.
Solve W = Fd problems for given force and distance, stating units.
Given a Sankey diagram, identify the useful and wasted branches.
Decide 'which Sankey conserves energy?' from a set, justifying the choice by checking the outputs sum to the input.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluency with the efficiency ratio and the work formula, and the ability to spot a conservation error in a Sankey, demonstrate the procedural outcomes.

constraints: Learners need prior fluency with percentages and proportional reasoning before this topic.

Quantitative efficiency/Sankey/work content is GCSE/KS4 (England) and HS-level in NGSS (HS-PS3-1, HS-PS3-3); KS3 and NGSS MS carry mainly qualitative precursors (e.g. energy is conserved; in an ideal, frictionless simple machine the product of force and displacement is unchanged, while real machines transfer less useful work out than is put in). Treat as a late-KS3 lead-in only with that caveat.
Keep work/energy (joules), force (newtons), and power (watts, a later topic) distinct with units and worked examples, since learners blur them.
Reading a fixed/tappable Sankey is a reference scaffold: it supports interpretation but does not provide the construct-and-calculate practice that is the main objective.
Recognition and calculation-answer items assess fluency but do not require learners to independently construct a to-scale Sankey diagram; include at least one build-from-scratch task.
When drawing Sankey diagrams, require a stated scale (e.g. 1 cm = 10 J) so proportionality is real and branch widths can be checked to sum to the input.
Always label the wasted branch as dissipated (usually to the thermal store of the surroundings), not destroyed, to keep conservation explicit.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original rated 3D and conversation formats as 'poor' with claims that '3D adds nothing' and 'dialogue doesn't build them'. These comparative/necessity claims are not established by the sources and have been dropped; the planar build-and-calculate task is proposed on its clear fit to proportional drawing and calculation, not on a universal law that other media cannot teach it. Spoken explanation (e.g. 'talk me through it') is used in the original diagnostic and is retained as a useful teaching move.

Corrected a feedback error that had labelled the useful output as 'the larger number'; useful output can never exceed total input, so efficiency ≤ 100% comes from useful being the smaller (or equal) quantity, not from any denominator rule. Also softened the over-100% feedback so inversion is given as the usual (not sole) cause.

The 100% energy-efficiency ceiling and the 'cannot drag past the input' behaviour are certain consequences of conservation of energy for any energy transfer; they are offered as optional interaction examples, not mandatory interface mechanisms. (A heat-pump COP >1 is a different ratio and not a counterexample.)

Two sources (NGSS placement and IOP Spark misconceptions) are marked verified:false in the row; the DfE statutory source is verified:true. Confidence should reflect that the misconception and HS-placement claims are unverified.
Arithmetic checked: efficiency 60/100 = 60%; W = 20 N × 2 m = 40 J; input 100 J = 60 J useful + 40 J wasted. All consistent.

probeDeeper: Your Sankey — do the wasted and useful arrows add back up to the input? What law says they must?
Could a machine ever be more than 100% efficient? What would that violate?
You held the load still for a minute — how much work did you do on it by the formula, and does that match your intuition?
Where does the 40 J of wasted energy actually GO, and how would you show that on the diagram?
assess.correctAnswer: Efficiency = useful/total × 100 = 60/100 = 60%. Sankey: one 100 J input arrow splitting into a 60 J useful arrow (straight on) and a 40 J wasted arrow (branching down, usually to thermal), widths in proportion and summing to the input. Work done = F × d = 20 N × 2 m = 40 J. Throughout, input energy equals useful plus wasted (energy conserved).

errorPatterns.pattern: Calculates efficiency as total/useful or the wrong ratio, giving over 100% ('120% efficient').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Efficiency is USEFUL out over TOTAL in; it can never exceed 100% because you can't get more useful energy out than you put in.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Watching the calculation — puts the larger number on top or divides the wrong way.

errorPatterns.pattern: Draws Sankey arrows that aren't proportional, or whose branches don't sum back to the input ('60 and 40 drawn the same width').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Set a scale (e.g. 1 cm = 10 J), measure each arrow to it, and check the branches add back to the input — energy is conserved.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Arrow widths ignore the numbers, or the input doesn't equal the sum of the outputs.

errorPatterns.pattern: Uses W = Fd with a distance not in the direction of the force, or computes work when nothing moves ('holding it still does work').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Work needs movement in the force's direction; no distance moved = no work done on the load; check the distance matches the force.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Plugs in the wrong distance, or claims work is done with zero movement.

responseLevels.gap: Gets efficiency the wrong way up (over 100%), draws non-proportional or unbalanced Sankey arrows, or misuses W=Fd.
responseLevels.full: Computes efficiency as useful/total, draws a scaled Sankey whose branches conserve the input, and applies W=Fd with the correct distance — explaining wasted energy as dissipated, not destroyed.
responseLevels.partial: Calculates efficiency and work correctly for the given numbers but draws the Sankey loosely (not to scale, or not quite balancing), or can't say where wasted energy goes.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are the figures for a motor: 100 J of electrical energy in, 60 J transferred usefully to lifting. Calculate its efficiency, draw a Sankey diagram to scale for this motor, then use W = Fd to find the work done lifting a 20 N load through 2 m. Talk me through it as you go. [Watch: efficiency = useful/total; wasted 40 J shown branching; arrows proportional and summing to the input; W = 20×2 = 40 J with units.]
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching the calculation and the drawing separates a child who applies useful/total, conserves energy in the Sankey (arrows proportional and summing) and uses W=Fd with the right distance, from one who gets efficiency over 100%, draws non-proportional arrows that don't balance, or misuses the work formula.
